jobs.description:
How to apply

Apply through the form below. It takes about 10 minutes. Along with your CV, it asks for:
a short message on why Abstract, why now and why you
one example of how you use AI at work

We read every application ourselves and reply within a week.
You will only be considered if you apply through the link below: https://abstractbio.notion.site/abstract-bio-careers
TLDR

We are building the biological inputs factory that will unlock AI for biology, starting from DNA, the first building block of every biomolecule. Demand for our first DNA product outran our capacity within months of launch, and we are now scaling 10x. As our Bioinformatics Engineer, you will own the sequencing data that tells us whether every molecule we make is right: the pipelines that QC each order, the analyses that show where our chemistry makes errors, and the tools that feed those answers back to R&D and production. The best candidate has 3-5 years working hands-on with sequencing data, ideally nanopore, ideally at a company that makes DNA. They are AI-native and scrappy, ship a working pipeline this week rather than a perfect one next quarter, and care about the molecule behind the reads. This is a sequencing-data role, not protein design or structural modelling. Your role will evolve with time; you should be excited by that and step up when needed. THIS IS NOT A 9 TO 5.

Story and mission

The Bessemer process made steel cheap and set off the Second Industrial Revolution. AI is now doing the same to biological design, and cloud labs and robots are doing it to testing. That pushes the bottleneck to the build step: the physical inputs. Every protein and every RNA starts as DNA, and DNA is still expensive. With current suppliers, the DNA to test one therapeutic antibody design costs around $100 per data point; a good antibody needs thousands of them, and a good antibody model needs millions. Abstract Bio is building the factory for those inputs, starting from DNA, the first building block.
We brought a DNA product, 4-10x cheaper than incumbents, to market within 6 months of founding the company. With a team of three and word of mouth alone, demand quickly outran our capacity, so we are now building for true scale. This means a 10x larger production platform, adding long and plasmid DNA, and starting the first R&D on RNA and proteins.
You cannot sell DNA you have not verified, and at 10x the volume you cannot verify it by eye. Every order needs to be sequenced, analysed and passed or failed automatically, and every failure needs to teach us something about our process. Building that is the job of the Bioinformatics Engineer. Our North Star is to be the biological inputs factory that gives scientists any biomolecule, on demand: the missing part of the stack that will unlock AI for biology.
Role description

We are turning DNA into a commodity, and a commodity wins on cost and reliability. Sequencing is how we prove reliability in production and get insights from R&D experiments. As our Bioinformatics Engineer, you make that measurement fast, automatic and cheap, and you turn the data behind it into insight that improves our process.
You are hands-on. You write the pipelines, read the alignments and look at the raw signal when the numbers do not add up. You work across R&D and production. When production needs to QC more orders, you build the pipeline that calls each one pass or fail without a human. When R&D changes the molecular biology, you show them exactly where the errors moved.
You are AI-native. Our lab will be built so that software can read it, and you are one of the people who make that true. You use AI to write and review code every day, and you build the tools and agents that let the rest of the team ask questions of our sequencing data.
You are scrappy. Off-the-shelf tools were built for genomes, not for millions of short synthetic molecules or a plate of plasmids. You will adapt the open-source tool, write your own when it does not exist.
You report to the founders and work side by side with the production and R&D teams. This is a ground-floor role: as we scale and add more data and software people, you will have the chance to grow into leading bioinformatics for a multi-site factory.
What you will do

Build the QC pipeline. Sequence-verify every order, from short DNA to long and plasmid DNA, with automated pass/fail calls and clear reports for customers.
Find where the errors come from. Characterise synthesis and assembly errors and tie them back to the method, the sequence and the run.
Close the loop with R&D. Turn error profiles into design rules.
Make sequencing cheap. Choose platforms, multiplexing and read depth so QC costs as little per base-pair as possible.
Connect the data. Wire sequencing results into our order and production data, and build the dashboards and agents that let anyone in the lab query them.

What you will need to succeed

Sequencing data. 3-5 years hands-on with sequencing reads (alignment, error calling, QC), in industry or a PhD.
AI-native. Solid Python, at home in a terminal, and you've built an AI tool people use.
Production pipelines. Nextflow, Snakemake or similar, running unattended.
Molecular biology sense. You can tell a chemistry error from a sequencing artefact.
Fast and calm. You ship the fix this week and explain results in plain language.

Nice-to-haves

Nanopore data, especially its error modes.
Time at a company that makes DNA.
Long-read or plasmid verification.
Bench time prepping sequencing libraries.

If you've read this far, start your motivation message with the word "Q30".

new_jobs.description:
How to apply

Apply through the form below. It takes about 10 minutes. Along with your CV, it asks for:
a short message on why Abstract, why now and why you
one example of how you use AI at work

We read every application ourselves and reply within a week.
You will only be considered if you apply through the link below: https://abstractbio.notion.site/abstract-bio-careers
TLDR

We are building the biological inputs factory that will unlock AI for biology, starting from DNA, the first building block of every biomolecule. Demand for our first DNA product outran our capacity within months of launch, and we are now scaling 10x. As our Bioinformatics Engineer, you will own the sequencing data that tells us whether every molecule we make is right: the pipelines that QC each order, the analyses that show where our chemistry makes errors, and the tools that feed those answers back to R&D and production. The best candidate has 3-5 years working hands-on with sequencing data, ideally nanopore, ideally at a company that makes DNA. They are AI-native and scrappy, ship a working pipeline this week rather than a perfect one next quarter, and care about the molecule behind the reads. This is a sequencing-data role, not protein design or structural modelling. Your role will evolve with time; you should be excited by that and step up when needed. THIS IS NOT A 9 TO 5.

Story and mission

The Bessemer process made steel cheap and set off the Second Industrial Revolution. AI is now doing the same to biological design, and cloud labs and robots are doing it to testing. That pushes the bottleneck to the build step: the physical inputs. Every protein and every RNA starts as DNA, and DNA is still expensive. With current suppliers, the DNA to test one therapeutic antibody design costs around $100 per data point; a good antibody needs thousands of them, and a good antibody model needs millions. Abstract Bio is building the factory for those inputs, starting from DNA, the first building block.
We brought a DNA product, 4-10x cheaper than incumbents, to market within 6 months of founding the company. With a team of three and word of mouth alone, demand quickly outran our capacity, so we are now building for true scale. This means a 10x larger production platform, adding long and plasmid DNA, and starting the first R&D on RNA and proteins.
You cannot sell DNA you have not verified, and at 10x the volume you cannot verify it by eye. Every order needs to be sequenced, analysed and passed or failed automatically, and every failure needs to teach us something about our process. Building that is the job of the Bioinformatics Engineer. Our North Star is to be the biological inputs factory that gives scientists any biomolecule, on demand: the missing part of the stack that will unlock AI for biology.
Role description

We are turning DNA into a commodity, and a commodity wins on cost and reliability. Sequencing is how we prove reliability in production and get insights from R&D experiments. As our Bioinformatics Engineer, you make that measurement fast, automatic and cheap, and you turn the data behind it into insight that improves our process.
You are hands-on. You write the pipelines, read the alignments and look at the raw signal when the numbers do not add up. You work across R&D and production. When production needs to QC more orders, you build the pipeline that calls each one pass or fail without a human. When R&D changes the molecular biology, you show them exactly where the errors moved.
You are AI-native. Our lab will be built so that software can read it, and you are one of the people who make that true. You use AI to write and review code every day, and you build the tools and agents that let the rest of the team ask questions of our sequencing data.
You are scrappy. Off-the-shelf tools were built for genomes, not for millions of short synthetic molecules or a plate of plasmids. You will adapt the open-source tool, write your own when it does not exist.
You report to the founders and work side by side with the production and R&D teams. This is a ground-floor role: as we scale and add more data and software people, you will have the chance to grow into leading bioinformatics for a multi-site factory.
What you will do

Build the QC pipeline. Sequence-verify every order, from short DNA to long and plasmid DNA, with automated pass/fail calls and clear reports for customers.
Find where the errors come from. Characterise synthesis and assembly errors and tie them back to the method, the sequence and the run.
Close the loop with R&D. Turn error profiles into design rules.
Make sequencing cheap. Choose platforms, multiplexing and read depth so QC costs as little per base-pair as possible.
Connect the data. Wire sequencing results into our order and production data, and build the dashboards and agents that let anyone in the lab query them.

What you will need to succeed

Sequencing data. 3-5 years hands-on with sequencing reads (alignment, error calling, QC), in industry or a PhD.
AI-native. Solid Python, at home in a terminal, and you've built an AI tool people use.
Production pipelines. Nextflow, Snakemake or similar, running unattended.
Molecular biology sense. You can tell a chemistry error from a sequencing artefact.
Fast and calm. You ship the fix this week and explain results in plain language.

Nice-to-haves

Nanopore data, especially its error modes.
Time at a company that makes DNA.
Long-read or plasmid verification.
Bench time prepping sequencing libraries.
